L’exil imposé d’un Canado-Algérien : l’h: A Canadian-Algerian’s Forced Exile: The Story of Lazhar Zouaïmia
Lazhar Zouaïmia est un homme libre; du m: Lazhar Zouaïmia is a free man; at least, as long as he doesn’t go back to Algeria.
Lazhar Zouaïmia nous raconte son histoir: Lazhar Zouaïmia tells us his story, two years after his imprisonment.
Le 19 février 2022, Lazhar Zouaïmia s’ap: On February 19, 2022, Lazhar Zouaïmia is getting ready to return to Canada, the country that took him in and the place he has considered home for nearly 20 years, after a trip to Algeria to visit his family. He has little idea, at that moment, that he will soon become a symbol of the Algerian regime’s repression.
À l’approche du cinquième anniversaire d: As the fifth anniversary of the Hirak approaches, the pro-democracy movement that swept through the streets of Algeria in February 2019, La Converse is publishing an audio documentary that looks back on this pivotal moment in the country’s history through the experience of Lazhar Zouaïmia. This Canadian of Algerian origin was imprisoned on February 19, 2022, at the end of a stay in his country of origin, because of his online activities.
Lazhar Zouaïmia habite en banlieue de Mo: Lazhar Zouaïmia has lived in the Montréal suburbs with his family for several years, but he has always kept a strong connection to Algeria, the country where he was born and where part of his family still lives. He made the “heartbreaking” choice to leave Algeria in 2003, disillusioned by the first years of Abdelaziz Bouteflika’s presidency. “I knew it wasn’t going to go anywhere. The people in power had no intention of doing anything [for the country],” he explains.
Il choisit donc d’immigrer au Québec, un: So he chose to immigrate to Quebec, a French-speaking land of “opportunity,” he says. After spending some time at the bedside of his daughter, then a newborn, he landed a job at Hydro-Québec as a technician, a position he still holds today.
En février 2022, Lazhar s’apprête à reto: In February 2022, Lazhar is preparing to go back to Algeria. “There had been a tragic event at home: the death of my child,” Lazhar tells La Converse’s microphone, remembering his son, Mehdi. “I wanted to visit my family, recharge, share my grief.”
Lazhar passe donc trois semaines dans sa: Lazhar spends three weeks with his family, near Annaba, a coastal city in the east, close to the Tunisian border. He also spends some time a little further south, in Ghardaïa, at the gateway to the Sahara. “I saw places I didn’t know before,” he says. “It did me good.”
On February 19, it is time to leave. Lazhar travels the 100 kilometres to Constantine airport to catch his morning flight to Algiers. From there, he is to take a plane to Montréal.
« Je suis passé au guichet pour obtenir: “I went to the counter to get my boarding pass,” he recalls. “There was a guy standing there [...]. He was looking at me. It was a bit strange.” He then realizes that something is about to happen.
Lorsque Lazhar obtient sa carte d’embarq: As soon as Lazhar gets his boarding pass, the man speaks. “He said to me: ‘Are you Lazhar Zouaïmia?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘You’re coming with us.’” Lazhar follows him, and an interrogation lasting several hours begins.
« J’étais stressé quand même, mais j’esp: “I was stressed, of course, but I was hoping it would end, [that] I would catch my plane to Algiers.” But as time goes by, hope dwindles. When boarding time comes and goes, anxiety sets in for good. His phone and tablet are confiscated, and the questions multiply.
« Ma conjointe m’a appelé parce que, en: “My wife called me because, in theory, I should have been in Algiers. [...] She said: ‘I’m worried.’ I answered: ‘Now you’re really worried. I’m with the security services.’” Hours later, Lazhar is taken outside the airport. He will spend the following night in detention.
« Ç’a été ma première nuit, ma première: “It was my first night, my first experience in a cell. No light, with bars, like the ones you see in movies.”
Pour comprendre l’emprisonnement de Lazh: To understand why Lazhar was imprisoned at that moment, we have to go back three years, to 2019. As the presidential election, scheduled for April, approached, the Algerian authorities announced in February that Abdelaziz Bouteflika, president since 1999, would run for a fifth term at the head of the country.
L’indignation est vive, la colère éclate: Outrage was intense, and anger erupted. Among other things, people denounced the fact that Bouteflika had been absent from public life since at least 2018. In fact, his appearances had gradually dwindled since 2013 because of serious health problems. Within days, citizens took to the streets to protest the news. The demonstrations resonated across Algeria, first in Kherrata, in Kabylie, on February 16, before sweeping through Algiers on February 22. That first massive demonstration marked the start of the Hirak.
Dès lors, chaque vendredi, le rendez-vou: From then on, the gathering was repeated every Friday. All over Algeria, people came out and declared their hope for democracy. This movement of unprecedented scale grew and reached the diaspora, including here in Canada.
« C’est comme si le peuple [algérien] ét: “It’s as if the [Algerian] people had been in a coma and woke up,” Lazhar Zouaïmia says. “They woke up to say no.” No to the continuation of Bouteflika’s rule, certainly, but above all, no to corruption and to the army’s prolonged grip on the state. “People were hopeful that things would change.”
À Montréal, des rassemblements hebdomada: In Montréal, weekly rallies, mirroring those organized thousands of kilometres away, were held in front of the Consulate General of Algeria in Montréal. Lazhar took part in the movement. A longtime member of Amnesty International, he participated in online forums and demonstrations in support of democracy in his country of origin.
D’après lui, c’est cette implication dan: In his view, it was this involvement in the movement that got him imprisoned. Lazhar is far from the only Hirak activist to have spent time in prison. “After 10 days [in prison], they took me to a special wing. It’s for active or passive terrorists; Facebook people, Hirak people and others, terrorists from the Black Decade.”
Loin de ses proches, il se retrouve donc: Far from his loved ones, he thus found himself locked up with terrorists for openly expressing his pro-democracy views. “It leaves scars. You lose weight, or you come out sick.”
Le cas de Lazhar appartient à une longue: Lazhar’s case is part of a long and sad tradition of repression under successive Algerian regimes. “Right after independence, political authoritarianism was already taking hold and the state’s repressive capacities were improving,” explains Francesco Cavatorta, a political science professor at Université Laval.
Le chercheur, qui a longtemps étudié le: The researcher, who has long studied the Maghreb, points out that in the aftermath of Algerian independence, the Front de libération nationale (FLN) quickly took on the role of sole party leading the country. For about thirty years, living conditions in Algeria improved: under the presidency of Houari Boumédiène in particular, the country invested heavily in education and health, propelled by a flourishing economy that depended on hydrocarbons.
Au tournant des années 1980, toutefois,: At the turn of the 1980s, however, Algeria was hit head-on by an economic crisis caused by the sudden drop in the price of oil. “People realized that the old economic system no longer worked,” says Cavatorta.
Des réformes s’ensuivent, mais l’insatis: Reforms followed, but dissatisfaction grew among the population. The FLN then attempted democratization, opening the door to a multiparty system in 1989. But after the anticipated victory of the Islamic Salvation Front, which advocates the creation of an Islamic state in Algeria, in the country’s first democratic elections in December 1991, the government panicked.
En janvier 1992, l’armée prend le contrô: In January 1992, the army took control of the country and cancelled the elections: the Black Decade then erupted, marked by a civil war pitting the Algerian army against Islamist terrorists, beginning in 1992. Ten years of terror punctuated by bloody clashes, in which, officially, the military and Islamist armed forces fought one another. Ten years of terrorism that would force a great many Algerians to leave their country in the hope of finding a better life elsewhere.
Pendant longtemps, la décennie noire va: For a long time, the Black Decade remained a “trauma” for the Algerian people, Cavatorta explains. So when the Hirak erupted in 2019, the population glimpsed a chance to finally establish a democracy that respected its will. “It becomes something of a moment when Algerian society rediscovers the street, rediscovers demonstrations, asks for something different,” says the expert.
Toutefois, l’arrivée de la COVID-19 frei: However, the arrival of COVID-19 slowed the movement. Public health measures quickly became a way for the Algerian regime to stifle demonstrations and, at the same time, Hirak activists. Little by little, a new era of repression set in.
« Le régime a visé beaucoup plus directe: “The regime targeted certain individuals much more directly, certain figures, certain journalists, certain activists.” Targeting certain nationals, such as Canadians of Algerian origin, is no accident: according to the professor, this method fits perfectly within the regime’s strategy.
« Ça indique assez clairement la volonté: “It signals quite clearly the regime’s intent, that is: ‘You’re expatriates, you’re no longer here. Stop sticking your nose in what no longer concerns you,’ in a way.”
Lazhar n’est pas le seul Canadien à avoi: Lazhar is not the only Canadian to have spent time behind bars during a trip to Algeria: Hadjira Belkacem, a home daycare educator in Montréal, was also turned back at the airport as she was about to board her flight home to Canada, in 2022. More recently, the case of researcher Raouf Farrah, arrested in February 2023 and held in prison for more than eight months, also drew a great deal of attention in media here.
Aux yeux de M. Cavatorta, ces cas sont d: In Cavatorta’s eyes, these cases have become something of an example of what can happen to nationals whose opinions displease the authorities. “The consequence is to make people who would like to run political campaigns, to push for change in the country from abroad, think twice. As we can see, being abroad doesn’t necessarily protect you – and it doesn’t protect the family who stays behind.”
Selon Lazhar, toutefois, baisser les bra: For Lazhar, however, giving up is not an option. “Repression leads nowhere,” he sums up. “Repressing people is not a solution. Many people came out, and they keep speaking, even in Algeria. [...] Some [people] are reconnecting a bit with a culture of resistance. There’s that heritage; people don’t like hogra*, as we say. It hits them, and they say: ‘I’m speaking now.’”
Au Québec aussi, des personnes ont pris: In Quebec too, people spoke out while Lazhar was in prison. “Fortunately, here [in Quebec], there was a big mobilization. I heard echoes of it, even in prison.” His circle gradually organized, and he received support from numerous institutions, such as the Syndicat de Champlain (teaching staff) and the Canadian Union of Public Employees, which represents him at Hydro-Québec.
Amnistie internationale organise aussi u: Amnesty International also organized a support campaign and mobilized to send him letters of solidarity. Jules Béliveau, a former neighbour and retired journalist, took the time to write him a letter that proved decisive in the fight for his release.
Dans le cadre de ce reportage, La Conver: For this report, La Converse brought the two men together to hear their reflections on the events of 2022, a year and a half after they happened.
Lorsque Jules Béliveau réfléchit à ses p: When Jules Béliveau thinks back on his first memories of Lazhar, he does so with a smile and immense respect. “When I found out, I have to tell you, I was floored,” he confides. “My neighbour, Lazhar, imprisoned in Algeria! A man who loved his country of origin so much, imprisoned there! It was extremely disturbing.”
Il décida alors de coucher ses pensées s: He then decided to put his thoughts on paper, for his friend. His letter was one of the many sent to Algeria in solidarity with Lazhar. “Writing a letter, in the end, isn’t very hard. Saying who Lazhar was to me isn’t hard. The quantity of letters that can land on a political leader’s desk, that’s what’s major.”
« Tout témoignage, toute action, quelle: “Every testimony, every action, whatever it is, matters,” Lazhar agrees. “[But] his testimony, all the same, carries a lot of weight. That’s not a drop in the bucket, eh! It’s not a drop!” Then, turning to Mr. Béliveau: “Your testimony carries weight in my situation.”
Soon, the letters multiplied. They gave him significant psychological support, and they also increased the pressure on the government to release him. After 40 days in detention, in late March 2022, he finally went back before the judge. A surprise awaited him when he returned to his cell.
« Après quelques minutes, le personnel d: “After a few minutes, the prison staff came to my cell. They said to me: ‘Get your things together.’ I didn’t understand. I had just come back in, how was I going to get [my things] together? They said: ‘No, you’re leaving!’” That’s when he understands what is happening: the judge has granted him provisional release. He is able to go home to his relatives, hundreds of kilometres away, near Annaba.
Même s’il est désormais en liberté provi: Even though he is now on provisional release, Lazhar’s troubles are not over. His first two attempts to leave the country, in April, fail: he is refused permission to leave the territory, through interminable detentions just before boarding his flight. A few weeks later, he tries a third time. The same scenario repeats itself: he is detained just before boarding, but this time, something changes.
« Après un certain temps, même le décoll: “After a while, even the plane’s takeoff is delayed,” he says. “And then they give me back my passport.” He avoids asking the officers in front of him any questions, not wanting to cause further trouble. He takes his luggage and hurries to the boarding gate.
« Je courais, pratiquement. J’étais le d: “I was practically running. I was the last [to board]. I had lost my belt, I was holding my pants on one side and my bag on the other!” he recounts with a small laugh. “And then, I got on. I took a photo and sent it to my wife, to show her I was on the plane.”
À Montréal, le retour est joyeux et empr: In Montréal, the homecoming is joyful and full of relief. Ululations ring out at Pierre-Elliott-Trudeau Airport. Lazhar arrives and takes his wife in his arms. “Thank you, everyone! Thank you, thank you,” we hear him say to the small crowd gathered to welcome him.
Lazhar est de nouveau un homme libre. Du: Lazhar is once again a free man. At least, as long as he doesn’t go back to Algeria. In October 2022, nearly six months after his return to Quebec, Algerian courts sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison, preventing him from returning to his country of origin without risking prison again, but this time for many years.
Après avoir vécu l’enfer en prison, Lazh: After living through the hell of prison, Lazhar nevertheless remains hopeful. He has turned his experience into a strength and a mission since returning to Quebec. Since then, he has been busy telling his story to shed light on human rights issues.
La Conversel’a accompagné lors d’une con: La Converse accompanied him to a conference organized by Amnesty International. Lazhar spoke to dozens of young people at Collège Lionel-Groulx, on Montréal’s North Shore.
« Le combat pour les droits humains néce: “The fight for human rights always requires commitment,” he explains on the way to the school. “It has become vital for me, especially since I went through this. It’s not theoretical, it’s not a faraway case. I lived it. So I’d really like people, through my case, to learn about other cases.”
Cette conférence, ce n’est pas la premiè: This is not the first talk Lazhar has given. He has told his story more than once, in the media but also to young people. Since his return, he has become familiar with large halls, audiences, and the exchanges that follow.
« C’est comme si c’est pas la première h: “It’s like, it’s not the first story like this I’ve heard,” says Laurence, a student at Lazhar’s talk. “I actually find that sad. It’s like we’ve gotten used to it, and we shouldn’t. Stories like this should keep moving us, keep making us sensitive and disappointed in the system.”
Toute action a son importance. Toute his: Every action matters. Every story has its lesson. For Lazhar Zouaïmia, telling his story is a duty. And his story is also that of Algeria, and of his wishes for its future. “Algeria is a country, it’s our country, it’s the people. We spent time there, we were born there, we have our ancestors, we have a history [there]. We wish it could be like other democratic countries.”
Son histoire porte ainsi l’espoir d’une: His story thus carries the hope of a new, renewed Algeria that reflects a rich heritage in all its nuances and lets its people decide their own future. “The first thing is for people to have their basic rights, [...] for people to have the right to speak. People are entitled to every right: to demonstrate, to assemble, to express themselves, the right of journalists to ask questions, the right to a fair justice system… That doesn’t require budgets, it requires will.”
